records.sourceFile: 50 years of research on the psychology of sport injury - A consensus statement.pdf

paper.citation: Tranaeus U, Gledhill A, Johnson U, Podlog L, Wadey R, Wiese Bjornstal DM, et al. 50 Years of Research on the Psychology of Sport Injury: A Consensus Statement. Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: Consensus statement by seven experts in the psychology of sport injury, summarising research on injury risk, rehabilitation and return to sport. The panel drew on literature from the 1980s to the present, rated evidence quality with a modified GRADE approach, and produced practitioner recommendations. The statement reports stress responses as the strongest psychological risk factor for acute injury, stress management and mindfulness interventions that reduced injuries in the studies reviewed, and competence, autonomy and relatedness as needs of returning athletes.
paper.tldr: Psychological factors matter across the injury pathway, and this consensus statement gives practitioners evidence-rated recommendations on injury risk, rehabilitation and return to sport. The strongest support is for stress management and mindfulness approaches to reduce injury risk, while the return-to-sport evidence is mostly cross-sectional, retrospective or qualitative.
paper.methods: Expert panel of seven researchers, each with at least 10 years of applied experience and 20 publications on sport injury psychology. The panel met digitally from May 2022 to July 2023 and in person in Stockholm in December 2022, with pairs drafting the risk, rehabilitation and return-to-sport sections. Literature was searched in five databases without an exhaustive protocol, evidence was rated with a modified GRADE approach, and three sports medicine practitioners reviewed the draft.
paper.findings: Among psychological factors, stress responses had the strongest relationship with acute injury risk in a systematic review cited by the panel, with evidence rated moderate for study design and consistency. Stress management and mindfulness interventions were reported to reduce injuries in all 12 intervention studies in Table 2 (samples of 20 to 401 athletes), and the panel rated this evidence moderate to high quality with high consistency. For return to sport, the panel rated the evidence on psychological factors as low to moderate quality, and identified competence, autonomy and relatedness as psychological needs that returning athletes commonly experience.
paper.limitations: The authors state the statement is not a systematic review and covers only English-language literature, with no Southern Hemisphere authors. The seven-person panel was selected by the lead author, and the statement excludes concussion and parasport. The intervention studies in Table 2 are small and report injury counts without pooled effect sizes, so the description of the reduction as clinically meaningful is the panel's judgment.
paper.practicalImplications: Screen athletes regularly for psychosocial stress, sleep quality and perceived recovery, and use mindfulness, acceptance-based or stress management approaches to reduce acute injury risk. In rehabilitation, allow time for social support and use cognitive-behavioural or acceptance-based coping programs. During return to sport, support competence, autonomy and relatedness, and keep clear lines of communication between athletes, coaches and medical staff.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the recommendation to screen for psychosocial stress, sleep and perceived recovery, and to build stress management and mindfulness practice into athlete routines. The statement does not report performance outcomes, and its support for these approaches comes from a small set of intervention studies.
paper.rtp: The return-to-sport recommendations are to build competence, autonomy and relatedness, to simulate the competitive environment progressively (for example, coaches simulating matches against lower-calibre opponents), and to keep communication clear across athletes, coaches and medical staff. The evidence for these is largely cross-sectional, retrospective or qualitative, so it should guide communication and readiness practice rather than set clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: A genome-wide association study for concussion risk.pdf

paper.citation: Kim SK, Roche MD, Fredericson M, Dragoo JL, Horton BH, Avins AL, et al. A genome-wide association study for concussion risk. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: A genome-wide scan of 4,064 concussion cases and 291,472 controls from two health-record biobanks identified two genetic variants, in SPATA5 and PLXNA4, associated with concussion. Previously proposed candidate genes, including ApoE4, were not associated with concussion in this larger dataset.
paper.tldr: Two rare genetic variants were linked to recorded concussion in large general-population biobanks, but candidate genes such as ApoE4 did not replicate. The findings are unreplicated and not athlete-specific, so they do not support genetic screening of athletes.
paper.methods: Concussion cases were identified from ICD-9/ICD-10 codes in Kaiser Permanente Northern California records (3,170 cases, 80,244 controls) and from primary care Read codes in UK Biobank (894 cases, 211,228 controls), restricted to European ancestry. Each cohort was analysed by logistic regression on imputed SNPs, adjusted for sex, height, weight and 10 principal components (plus age in UK Biobank), and the two cohorts were combined by fixed-effects meta-analysis with a genome-wide threshold of p < 7.7x10-9. Previously reported candidate gene variants were also tested.
paper.findings: rs144663795 in SPATA5 (OR 2.91 per allele copy, p = 9.7x10-11) and rs117985931 in PLXNA4 (OR 3.59, p = 3.97x10-9) were associated with concussion, with risk allele frequencies of 1.4% and 0.13% in UK Biobank; the authors caution that the PLXNA4 signal is close to the threshold. ApoE4 (p = 0.19), rs405509 (p = 0.31) and variants in BDNF, DRD4, SLC17A7 and NGF were not associated (p > 0.05), and ApoE2 was borderline (p = .067). Concussion was recorded in 3.8% of the Kaiser cohort but only 0.42% of UK Biobank.
paper.limitations: Concussion was defined from diagnosis codes, likely under-recorded, with no information on mechanism, prior concussions or symptom severity, and sport-related concussions could not be separated from other causes. The analysis was limited to European ancestry, the associations have not been validated in an independent cohort, and the lead author leads a sports-injury genetic testing company. The discussion of sex, height and weight effects names the same cohort (described as RPGEH and as KPRB) for opposite results, so that passage cannot be interpreted reliably.
paper.practicalImplications: The study does not support using these markers to screen athletes, restrict sport choice or change concussion management, because the cohorts were not athletes and the results are unreplicated. It does suggest that single candidate-gene findings, such as ApoE4, should not be used to judge an athlete's concussion risk.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured concussion diagnoses only and has no performance outcomes, so it cannot inform training or performance decisions.
paper.rtp: The study did not examine recovery or return to play, and the authors list recovery time as future work. It cannot be used to guide concussion clearance or return-to-play timing.

records.sourceFile: A narrative review of psychiatric features of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome as conceptualized in the 20th century.pdf

paper.citation: Iverson GL, Kissinger-Knox A, Huebschmann NA, Castellani RJ, Gardner AJ. A narrative review of psychiatric features of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome as conceptualized in the 20th century. Front Neurol 2023;14:1214814.
paper.abstract: This narrative review re-examined case descriptions of 155 boxers from 21 articles published between 1928 and 1999. It tested whether psychiatric problems were described as clinical features of 20th-century chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Psychiatric problems were recorded in 34.8% of cases, but only 6.5% were described as primarily psychiatric. The authors conclude that depression, suicidality and anxiety were not clinical features of the condition, which supports the 2021 consensus criteria dropping them.
paper.tldr: Psychiatric problems were noted in about a third of 20th-century boxers, but usually alongside neurological signs and rarely as the main problem. The authors argue that depression, suicidality and anxiety should not be treated as features of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome.
paper.methods: Narrative review of clinical descriptions in 21 articles from 1928 to 1999, drawn from three earlier reviews. Two authors reviewed each article, extracted quotes and coded cases for psychiatric features. Duplicate and non-boxer cases were excluded, leaving 155 boxers, and results are reported as frequencies and percentages.
paper.findings: Of 155 boxers, 34.8% had a psychiatric, neuropsychiatric or neurobehavioural problem recorded, and 6.5% were described as primarily psychiatric. Documented rates were 11.0% for depression, 0.6% (one case) for suicidality, 3.9% for anxiety, 20.0% for anger control problems and 25.2% for personality change. The authors also cite a separate 2021 study of 336 brain donors, which found no association between these psychiatric features and CTE neuropathologic change.
paper.limitations: Case descriptions record a feature only when authors mention it, so 44.5% to 87.7% of cases are coded as unknown or not mentioned for each feature. The text gives anger control problems as 19.0%, but Table 5 gives 20.0% (31 cases); this summary uses the table value. The claim that psychiatric features are not associated with CTE neuropathology rests on the separate 2021 brain-donor study, not on this review's data.
paper.practicalImplications: Depression, anxiety or suicidal thoughts in a former contact-sport athlete should be assessed for the usual causes seen in the general population, since the authors argue these features do not point to traumatic encephalopathy syndrome. Staff should not treat mood or behaviour change as evidence of the neurological condition without the clinical signs the historical cases describe, such as dysarthria, gait disturbance and cognitive decline.
paper.athleteDev: The review has no direct performance application. Because it concerns former boxers with established neurological damage, its findings should not be used to read mood or behaviour changes in current athletes as signs of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome.
paper.rtp: The review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions, since it studies historical case descriptions and does not examine return to play or its criteria. The authors argue that psychiatric features should not raise the level of certainty of underlying pathology in the consensus criteria, so they should not be used alone to support a diagnosis that bears on an athlete's future participation.

records.sourceFile: A review of the personality traits in post-concussion syndrome.pdf

paper.citation: Mavroudis I, Chatzikonstantinou S, Petridis F, Balmus IM, Ciobica A. A review of the personality traits in post-concussion syndrome. Acta Neurologica Belgica. 2024.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of 16 studies on whether personality traits predict post-concussion syndrome after mild traumatic brain injury. The authors report that emotional reserve, cognitive resilience and lower somatic trait anxiety were linked to better outcomes, while anxiety sensitivity, pain catastrophizing, helplessness and sports-concussion symptom load were linked to worse outcomes. Parental anxiety was not linked to persistent symptoms in children, and the authors call for further research on samples that include healthy comparison groups.
paper.tldr: Traits such as resilience, somatic trait anxiety and anxiety sensitivity appear to relate to whether concussion symptoms persist. The evidence is mostly from non-athlete samples, so use it to flag possible risk rather than to set athlete screening thresholds.
paper.methods: Review with narrative synthesis of 16 studies identified by searching PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to April 2023, plus reference lists. Two authors screened titles, abstracts and full texts, and study quality was rated with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, with no quality concerns reported. Studies were grouped by personality trait because designs and outcome measures varied, and no pooled analysis was done.
paper.findings: In a 1-year mTBI cohort of 122 patients, lower psychological resilience, higher somatic trait anxiety, embitterment and mistrust were linked to persistent symptoms, and in 61 mTBI patients anxiety sensitivity and alexithymia were correlated with more post-concussion symptoms. In 332 adolescents and young adults with sport-related concussion, lower resilience was linked to more symptoms and delayed recovery. In 98 children with concussion, parental anxiety was not associated with persistent symptoms at 1 month, although parents of persistently symptomatic children remained more anxious; these are observational associations, not tested predictive models.
paper.limitations: Most included samples are general mTBI populations such as falls, road traffic and trauma patients, three samples are healthy volunteers, and sport-related samples are a small subset. The authors note small samples and reliance on self-report, and designs and measures vary. Reporting is inconsistent: the abstract lists four databases while the methods list three, the abstract mentions polygenic risk score analyses and a publication-bias analysis that are not presented, Table 1 cites reference 13 for two different studies, and its row for the 329-athlete meta-analysis repeats results reported for another study.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that psychological resilience, somatic trait anxiety, embitterment and mistrust be considered when assessing risk of persistent symptoms after concussion, and that anxiety sensitivity and alexithymia may be worth identifying early. Treat these as risk markers from mostly non-athlete studies rather than validated screening tools or cut-offs. One included study suggests that children whose symptoms last at least 1 month may benefit from neuropsychological care alongside usual concussion management.
paper.athleteDev: The review is about symptom persistence after concussion, not performance. Its one performance-adjacent finding is that lower resilience was linked to more symptom aggravation during physical or cognitive activity in young people with sport-related concussion, which is not a performance measure.
paper.rtp: The review does not set return-to-play criteria. Its personality findings may help flag athletes at higher risk of persistent symptoms, but they cannot be used as a clearance tool or to decide when an athlete can return to sport.
